# Results — Study 42 (Last-Call): the turn-of-the-month effect, 1950–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily total return of the **S&P 500
(^GSPC)** 1950–2026 for the effect, and **SPY** 1993–2026 for the tradable/cost run. Turn-of-the-month
= the [-1, +3] window (last trading day of a month + first three of the next). As-of **2026-06-11**;
^GSPC inputs fingerprint `54fd9e780da2`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Still alive?" `FADED`

The concentration is **real and large**: on the S&P 500, the four turn-of-the-month days (≈19% of all
days) earned **11.0 bp/day** against **1.9 bp/day** the rest of the time — a Welch t of **5.1** across
76 years. But it is `MIRAGE` to *trade*: a long-the-window-else-cash rule on SPY makes **4.3% a year
(Sharpe 0.55)** against buy-and-hold's **10.8% (Sharpe 0.64)** — you sacrifice 60% of the return to sit
in cash 81% of the time, and 12 round-trips a year of costs only widen the gap. And the effect has
`FADED`: the TOM premium fell from **13.8 bp/day (1950–87)** to **4.8 bp/day (2008–on)**, where it is
now statistically indistinguishable from the **4.1 bp/day** of an ordinary day. A textbook anomaly
that is real, uneconomic, and nearly arbitraged away.

## Data stamp

- **Effect**: S&P 500 (^GSPC) daily, 1950 → 2026, 19,232 days, fingerprint `54fd9e780da2`
- **Tradable**: SPY daily, 1993 → 2026

## The effect is real and large

| | mean return | n days |
|---|---|---|
| turn-of-the-month days ([-1,+3]) | **11.0 bp/day** | 3,672 |
| all other days | **1.9 bp/day** | 15,559 |
| every day | 3.7 bp/day | 19,232 |

Welch t for the difference: **5.1**. The ~19% of days in the window carry the lion's share of the
market's drift — this is not noise, it's one of the most replicated calendar facts in finance.

## …and yet trading it loses to buy-and-hold (SPY, 1993–2026)

| | CAGR | Sharpe | max-DD | time in market |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TOM-only, 0 bp | +4.3% | 0.55 | −29% | 19% |
| TOM-only, 2 bp | +3.8% | 0.50 | −30% | 24% |
| TOM-only, 5 bp | +3.1% | 0.41 | −30% | 24% |
| **Buy & hold SPY** | **+10.8%** | **0.64** | −55% | 100% |

A higher *per-day* return doesn't make a strategy: out of the market four-fifths of the time, the
TOM-only book compounds far less, and its Sharpe still trails buy-and-hold. The drawdown is shallower
only because it's usually in cash — the same exposure-reduction illusion as the January Barometer
([Study 41](../../41-hangover/)).

## …and it has faded since it was published

| | TOM days | non-TOM days |
|---|---|---|
| 1950–1987 | **13.8 bp** | 0.7 bp |
| 1988–2007 | 11.4 bp | 2.3 bp |
| 2008–on | **4.8 bp** | 4.1 bp |

By the modern sample the turn-of-the-month day earns essentially what any other day earns. McConnell &
Xu (2008) documented the effect's strength; the years since show its decay — the McLean–Pontiff fade in
one of its cleanest forms.

## The honest takeaway

The turn-of-the-month effect is a `REAL`, large, decades-robust seasonal — and a `MIRAGE` to trade: a
window-only book underperforms buy-and-hold (you forfeit the other 81% of days), costs erode the thin
edge, and the premium has `FADED` to an ordinary day's return since ~2008. A beautiful fact that does
not pay.
